name: Yusuf Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won’t be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the stroke rehabilitation ward at Kingsmoor Hospital. Our patients have had a stroke and are past the dangerous first days, so my job is getting them back to living: helping them wash and dress with one working arm, practising swallowing safely, getting them on their feet with the physios, and keeping their spirits up. Twelve-hour days, some nights. It's slow work and you see small wins every day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the small wins, like a man feeding himself for the first time in three weeks. I use AI every day, for translating with Arabic-speaking families, for patient exercise sheets in simple words, and I tutor nursing students online on Sunday evenings using it. What wears me out is money. My wife Amira is a care worker in an old people's home, we rent a small flat, we want children, and we've got maybe three weeks of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out as it's written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay. I'd be a bit surprised, but I can picture it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we were sold too much too fast, and that good tools still help if you know how to use them. I'd keep using the ones that work, quietly. I'm not one to post my opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI turns out to be hype, I've lost a few evenings learning apps. My patients still need someone to teach them to hold a spoon again. The real pressure for us is the rent and wanting a baby on two low wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shifts and keep the Sunday tutoring going, which brings in about 150 a month. I'd try to put that tutoring money aside every month instead of spending it. I'd keep using the translation app on the ward, because it's already better than waiting for an interpreter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, a little disappointed. Mostly thinking about money and family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Amira say about a baby in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd say next year, like we've said for two years. We need about three months' rent saved before we'd feel right. My mother keeps asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine work you'd be glad AI took?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The falls and pressure sore forms. We fill in the same boxes every shift. If AI did that, I'd have twenty more minutes for walking practice.

I'd keep using **useful tools** quietly rather than post opinions.
think: AI flopping costs me only a few **evenings** learning apps.
The real pressure is **rent** and wanting a baby on two low wages.
do: Keep his shifts and the **Sunday tutoring** worth about 150 a month.
Save the **tutoring money** every month instead of spending it.
Keep using the **translation app** with families on the ward.
feel: **Steady**, a little disappointed, and focused on **family** money.

fieldNote: His job is secure; the unease is about **starting a family** on thin savings.
He already earns a **side income** from online tutoring.
He values AI for **translation** with families, a practical everyday use.

steps.text: Keep tutoring nursing students online on Sunday evenings
Save the 150 a month of tutoring money
Keep using the translation app with Arabic-speaking families

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I expect, honestly. A lot of it is already here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time for people willing to learn, and that we should use it to free nurses for patients. I'd say families and communities should help each other through the changes, not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife washes and feeds old people for a living, and I teach stroke patients to walk. Between us, we're the last people a robot reaches. The paperwork changes, but our hands are safe for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the ward manager to trial the AI speech therapy app for our patients, the one I've seen at a conference. I'd keep tutoring and add another evening. I'd also start sketching the idea I've had for a while: simple home exercise videos for stroke patients, made with AI, sold to clinics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, but excited. I like change when I can see where it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ward clerk, Dennis, and the discharge planners. Booking transport and chasing forms is exactly what the card says goes first. Dennis has been there since before I was born.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're excited about a business. Can you afford to try it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. But AI makes it cheap to start: a phone, a free editing app, my evenings. If it fails, I've lost time, not money.

I'd urge **families and communities** to help each other, not wait for government.

Plan **home exercise videos** for stroke patients to sell to clinics.
feel: **Uneasy** about money but **excited** by change he can see.

fieldNote: He sees the **household** as well protected because both jobs are hands-on.

He'd bring **AI tools** into the ward himself, not wait to be told.

steps.text: Ask the ward manager to trial an AI speech therapy app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028, then robots in 2031. That's quick. I'd need to move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who wait will be hurt, and people who move will be okay. I'd say the government should back apprenticeships and small businesses, not just hand out money. I'd say it at the mosque, to the young men especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years of warning is enough for me to build something of my own before the robots get to rehab in 2031. The thinking parts of my job go in 2028, which is fine. But in 2031 both my job and Amira's are in reach. We'd have three years after the AGI part to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the exercise video business straight away, evenings and weekends, and aim for my first clinic customer within six months. I'd do the hospital's course on robot-assisted rehab, so I'm the one who sets up the machines. We'd put off a baby until 2029, which is hard. And every penny of tutoring money would go into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a driven way. Like the start of a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for you and Amira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's our runway. Both our jobs are mostly hands, so we've got until about 2031. If I can get the business paying in that time, we've got something that isn't a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting off a baby. What would Amira say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say she doesn't want to wait forever. We'd argue, then agree on a date, 2029. My mother would tell us to trust God and get on with it.

I'd urge government to back **apprenticeships** and small businesses, not handouts.

Take the hospital's **robot-assisted rehab** course to run the machines.

feel: **Anxious** but **driven**, like the start of a race.
S2.quote: Two years of warning is enough for me to build something of my own before the robots get to rehab in 2031.
fieldNote: He treats the **three-year gap** as a runway, not a reprieve.
He expects **both jobs** to be at risk from 2031 but feels in control.

steps.text: Start the stroke exercise video business and find a clinic customer
Take the hospital's robot-assisted rehab course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 for AGI and robots around 2034. Five years. That's a good amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and that families and businesses should plan now. I'd say young people should get practical skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd spend my savings on the business, not a bigger flat, because a flat won't feed us when the robots come. I'd be 35 when robots reach rehab. That's young enough to run something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the video business slowly and put the first 1,000 I save into equipment and a proper website. I'd do the robot-assisted rehab course in year two or three. And we'd try for a baby in 2028, once the business is earning even a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't putting your savings into a business risky, with so little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. But the other choice is waiting with my savings until robots come, and then what? I'd rather risk 1,000 now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. Nursing pays the rent while the business grows. Maybe later, if it works.

I'd tell young people to get **practical skills**.

fieldNote: He's comfortable **risking savings**, rare for someone this short of money.

steps.text: Invest the first 1,000 saved in video equipment and a website

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036 and robots around 2039. Ten years. That's a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where hard workers win. I'd say businesses and families can plan, and government should help with training. I'd say it with a smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather be the nurse who teaches the rehab robot than the one it replaces. Ten years is enough time to start a family and build a business. That actually looks good for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have our first child in the next year or two. I'd grow the video business slowly, then offer clinics help setting up AI rehab tools. I'd volunteer for every new technology trial on the ward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. Calm, for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your child about work, one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn with your hands and your head. My father fixed cars without a manual. I'd like to think I can learn whatever comes, as long as I'm allowed to earn while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the money worry go away in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not fully. But with ten years, the business has time to grow. That changes how I sleep.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to build the business and no savings, and Amira and I would both be in the robots' path by 2031. What would help is apprenticeships and small business loans for people like us, and training that pays while you learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about community. At our mosque, people help each other find work. That will matter more than any government scheme.

headlineQuote: My father fixed cars without a manual. I'd like to think I can learn whatever comes, as long as I'm allowed to earn while I learn.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old stroke rehab nurse** who uses AI every day.
He's married to Amira, a **care worker**, and they want children but have little saved.
He tutors nursing students online and dreams of a **video business** for stroke patients.
He's **anxious** under fast AGI but always has a plan, and calm with ten years.
He favours **apprenticeships**, family and community over government handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to build a business before robots reach both their jobs.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** and small business loans for people like them.
